paragraphs.heading: Between conductor and insulator
paragraphs.text: A semiconductor is a material that carries electricity better than an insulator but not as well as a conductor. Silicon, germanium and gallium arsenide are examples, along with elements close to the so-called metalloid staircase of the periodic table. Silicon is key to building most electronic circuits. Gallium arsenide is the second most common semiconductor after it, used in laser diodes, solar cells and microwave-frequency integrated circuits.

paragraphs.heading: Changing conductivity on purpose
paragraphs.text: A semiconductor's conductivity can be changed by adding impurities to its crystal, a process called doping. Doping greatly raises the number of charge carriers. In silicon, adding about one atom in 10⁸ of phosphorus, arsenic or antimony, or of boron, gallium or indium, increases conductivity, and the result is called an extrinsic semiconductor. Heating a semiconductor also raises its conductivity, the reverse of a metal, which conducts less as it warms.

paragraphs.heading: n-type and p-type
paragraphs.text: Doping with Group V elements makes them act as donors that supply free electrons, which is called n-type doping. Doping with Group III elements makes them act as acceptors that create free holes, which is p-type doping. The two labels refer to an excess of electrons and a shortage of them. Materials for electronic devices are doped under precise conditions to control where each type goes, and a hot-point probe can quickly tell which type a sample is.

paragraphs.heading: What happens at a junction
paragraphs.text: When two regions with different doping sit in the same crystal, they form a junction. Picture germanium with a p-doped part and an n-doped part: the n side holds extra electrons and the p side extra holes, and the two trade carriers. Electrons drifting from the n side meet holes drifting from the p side and are removed by recombination until a balance is reached. What remains is a narrow strip of fixed ions, which sets up an electric field across the junction.

paragraphs.heading: From junctions to devices
paragraphs.text: Diodes, transistors and most of today's electronics rest on how charge carriers behave at these junctions. Semiconductor devices can let current pass more easily one way than the other, vary their resistance, or react to light or heat. Since doping, electric fields and light can all change a semiconductor's electrical properties, devices made from them can amplify signals, switch, and convert energy. In some semiconductors, excited electrons give off light rather than heat, and these are used to build light-emitting diodes and fluorescent quantum dots.

paragraphs.heading: A short history
paragraphs.text: Some semiconductor properties were noticed between the middle of the 1800s and the early decades of the 1900s. Their first practical use in electronics was the cat's-whisker detector of 1904, a crude diode used in early radio receivers. Advances in quantum physics then brought the transistor in 1947, followed by the integrated circuit in 1958.
